title: What competency assessment does CLIA require for lab personnel?
description: The six CLIA competency procedures in 42 CFR 493, who must be assessed, the semiannual then annual frequency, and who may assess, as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: The Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments (CLIA) regulations at 42 CFR Part 493 require laboratories doing moderate or high complexity testing to assess the competency of everyone who tests patient specimens, using six specified procedures for each test. Assessment is due twice in the first year of testing, then at least annually, and again before reporting results after a change in method or instrument. Waived-only laboratories are exempt from this federal requirement.
keyTakeaways: The six procedures are listed in 42 CFR 493.1413(b)(8) for moderate complexity testing and 493.1451(b)(8) for high complexity testing, and apply to every test a person performs.

Frequency is at least semiannually during the first year an individual tests patient specimens, then at least annually, plus reevaluation before reporting results when methodology or instrumentation changes.
Only people qualified as a technical consultant, technical supervisor or general supervisor may perform competency assessments of testing personnel, according to CMS guidance revised in May 2025.
CMS states that training, performance appraisals and proficiency testing alone do not satisfy the documented competency assessment requirement.

A CMS proposed rule published October 8, 2026 would remove the separate competency procedures for provider-performed microscopy; comments close December 7, 2026. It would not change annual competency assessment for other nonwaived testing.
regulator: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), US Department of Health and Human Services, with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
appliesTo: Laboratories holding a CLIA certificate that perform moderate complexity or high complexity (nonwaived) testing, including hospital, reference and physician office laboratories
Testing personnel, and technical consultants, technical supervisors, general supervisors and clinical consultants assessed against their regulatory duties
Laboratories performing provider-performed microscopy (PPM) procedures, under a modified set of procedures

sections.heading: Which laboratories and staff must have a CLIA competency assessment?

blocks.text: Every laboratory that performs moderate or high complexity testing must assess and document the competency of all personnel who perform that testing. The general rule is in [42 CFR 493.1235](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-IV/subchapter-G/part-493/subpart-K/section-493.1235), which requires the laboratory to "establish and follow written policies and procedures to assess employee and, if applicable, consultant competency." The detailed duties sit in Subpart M, Personnel, as responsibilities of the technical consultant, technical supervisor and general supervisor.

Laboratories that perform only waived tests are outside the federal requirement. The CMS brochure [Assessing Personnel Competency](https://www.cms.gov/regulations-and-guidance/legislation/clia/downloads/clia_compbrochure_508.pdf) (revised May 2025) says CLIA does not require a competency assessment for testing personnel in waived-only laboratories, although it calls the practice good laboratory practice and expects staff to be trained to follow manufacturers' instructions. Accrediting organizations can set stricter rules for waived testing; see [Joint Commission competency expectations](/regulations/joint-commission-staff-competency-requirements).

CMS also expects documented competency assessments for clinical consultants, technical consultants, technical supervisors and general supervisors, measured against their own Subpart M responsibilities. If any of them also perform testing, the six testing procedures apply to them as well. This page states the position as at November 2026, based on the eCFR text current to November 5, 2026.

sections.heading: What are the six required competency assessment procedures?

blocks.text: The six procedures are set out in the technical consultant duties at [42 CFR 493.1413(b)(8)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-IV/subchapter-G/part-493/subpart-M/section-493.1413) and repeated, word for word, in the technical supervisor duties at [42 CFR 493.1451(b)(8)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-IV/subchapter-G/part-493/subpart-M/section-493.1451). CMS says all six apply to every test a person performs, even when several tests run on one platform.

Observation record for the maintenance and function checks the person performs.
(v) Test performance
Testing previously analyzed specimens, internal blind samples or external proficiency testing samples.
Results compared with expected values, with acceptance criteria stated in advance.
(vi) Problem solving
Assessment of problem solving skills.
Written or oral case questions, or a documented troubleshooting event.

blocks.text: For provider-performed microscopy, the laboratory director's duties at 42 CFR 493.1359(c) list five procedures. Observation of instrument maintenance does not apply. CMS's brochure confirms that PPM assessments need only five of the six.

sections.heading: How often must CLIA competency be assessed?

blocks.text: Competency must be evaluated and documented at least semiannually during the first year an individual tests patient specimens, and at least annually after that. Paragraph (b)(9) of both 493.1413 and 493.1451 adds a third trigger: if test methodology or instrumentation changes, the individual's performance must be reevaluated, including use of the new method or instrument, "prior to reporting patient test results."

blocks.title: CMS guidance on frequency
blocks.text: "You must perform a competency assessment for all personnel who perform laboratory testing at least once a year. All six procedures must be documented for each of these personnel each year." CMS, Assessing Personnel Competency, revised May 2025.

The first year clock starts when the person begins testing patient specimens in that laboratory, not on their hire date. A person moving to a new laboratory starts a new first year there. CMS suggests spreading the procedures across the year by building them into routine work, which also gives more realistic observation. For setting the dates in a learning system, see [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles).

sections.heading: Who is allowed to perform CLIA competency assessments?

blocks.text: The assessor must hold the qualifications of the role that owns the duty. In moderate complexity testing, that is the technical consultant or someone who meets technical consultant qualifications. In high complexity testing, the technical supervisor may delegate the duty in writing to a general supervisor who meets the qualification requirements; [42 CFR 493.1463(b)(4)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-IV/subchapter-G/part-493/subpart-M/section-493.1463) lists "evaluating and documenting the competency of all testing personnel" among the duties that may be delegated to the general supervisor.

CMS states plainly that personnel who do not meet the regulatory qualifications of a technical consultant, technical supervisor or general supervisor "cannot perform or be designated to perform competency assessments." A peer observer with less qualification can gather information, but the qualified person must review and sign off. The laboratory director remains ultimately responsible. Where the director is the only person testing, CMS expects the director to set and document a minimum proficiency level, for example through proficiency testing samples or external review.

sections.heading: How is competency assessment different from training and proficiency testing?

blocks.text: Training builds the skill before testing starts, while competency assessment checks afterwards that the person follows procedures and gets correct results. CMS says training and personnel evaluations "do not satisfy the CLIA requirement for a documented laboratory competency assessment." The training duty itself is separate: 493.1413(b)(7) and 493.1451(b)(7) require each person performing tests to receive "regular in-service training and education appropriate for the type and complexity of the laboratory services performed."

Proficiency testing results can feed procedure (v), but CMS states that proficiency testing alone cannot cover all six procedures. A useful way to separate the three activities is with the [competency assessment](/glossary/competency-assessment) and [verification of competency](/glossary/verification-of-competency) definitions: training is the input, competency assessment is the check against a stated standard, and proficiency testing is one external data point.

sections.heading: What records are needed, and are the CLIA rules changing?

blocks.text: The regulations require competency to be documented but do not set a separate retention period for competency records in Subpart M. The general laboratory retention standard at [42 CFR 493.1105](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-IV/subchapter-G/part-493/subpart-J/section-493.1105) sets a minimum of 2 years for most records, including quality system assessment records. Many laboratories keep competency files for at least two full assessment cycles so an inspector can see the first year semiannual pattern and the annual cycle.

blocks.title: Proposed: not in force as at November 2026
blocks.text: A CMS and CDC proposed rule published October 8, 2026 (91 FR 64480) would rescind the laboratory director's PPM competency procedures at 493.1359(c)(1) through (5) and the PPM semiannual and annual evaluation at 493.1359(d). The proposal states it would not change requirements for personnel training or annual competency assessment for other testing. Comments close December 7, 2026.

Laboratories with PPM testing should keep assessing under the current rule until a final rule is published. For record structure, see [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit).

sections.heading: What does a compliant competency calendar look like for one person?

blocks.text: A workable calendar ties each assessment to the person's first patient testing date and to each test system they run. The illustrative plan below is for a new medical technologist in a high complexity chemistry section and should be adapted to the laboratory's own procedures.

blocks.text: Tracking this per person and per test system is a [training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) problem: rows are people, columns are test systems, and each cell holds the date of the last six-procedure assessment and the next due date.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models each test system, the six assessment procedures and the qualified assessor roles as linked elements, so a gap such as a missing problem solving assessment for one analyzer shows up before an inspection. When a method changes, the people who run that test can be identified from those links and scheduled for reevaluation. See how this works for [healthcare and life sciences organizations](/industries/healthcare-life-sciences).

faqs.q: Do all six procedures have to be done for every test?
faqs.a: Yes, for moderate and high complexity testing. CMS guidance states the six procedures apply to all personnel who perform these tests and for every test performed, even when multiple tests run on a single platform. Laboratories often group tests by test system and document all six procedures for each system, provided each test is covered.

faqs.q: Can a coworker perform the direct observation?
faqs.a: Only if that person meets the qualification requirements of a technical consultant, technical supervisor or general supervisor, as applicable to the testing complexity. CMS states that personnel who lack those qualifications cannot perform or be designated to perform competency assessments. Others may help collect information, but a qualified person must perform the assessment.

faqs.q: Does CLIA require competency assessment for waived testing?
faqs.a: No. CMS states that CLIA does not require a competency assessment for testing personnel in laboratories performing only waived testing, though staff must be trained to follow manufacturers' instructions. Accreditation standards can be stricter: Joint Commission's waived testing goal for hospitals expects competence to be assessed at orientation and annually.

faqs.q: Is an annual performance appraisal enough?
faqs.a: No. CMS says personnel evaluations rate behaviors and attributes related to the job and differ from competency assessment. A performance appraisal does not satisfy the requirement for a documented assessment using the six procedures, although both can be completed in the same review meeting if the competency record stands on its own.

factCheck.claim: 493.1235: laboratory must establish and follow written policies and procedures to assess employee and, if applicable, consultant competency.

493.1413(b)(7)-(9): regular in-service training; six competency procedures (i) to (vi); evaluation at least semiannually in first year, then at least annually, and reevaluation before reporting after methodology or instrumentation change. eCFR current to 2026-11-05.
493.1451(b)(7)-(9): identical six procedures and frequency for high complexity testing.
493.1463(b)(4): director or technical supervisor may delegate to the general supervisor evaluating and documenting the competency of all testing personnel.
493.1359(c)-(d) PPM: five procedures (no instrument maintenance observation); semiannual in first year then annual (read in full part 493 text, eCFR 2026-11-05).
493.1105: records retention minimum 2 years for most laboratory records including quality system assessment records.

CMS brochure (revised May 2025): waived-only labs not required to assess TP competency; training and personnel evaluations do not satisfy requirement; six procedures for every test; all six documented each year; semiannual in first year; PT alone insufficient; CC, TC, TS, GS need competency assessment; only TC/TS/GS-qualified personnel may assess; LD sole tester sets minimum proficiency level.

Proposed rule 91 FR 64480 (October 8, 2026): proposes rescinding 493.1359(c)(1)-(5) and (d); states it would not change personnel training or annual competency assessment requirements; comments due December 7, 2026.
